plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a scene diagram of an airplane sighting two points on a straight highway below it. A small colored drawing of a jetliner sits at the upper left, nose pointed left, and a teal dashed horizontal line runs to the right from the aircraft to stand for the horizontal at flight altitude. Across the lower part of the figure a solid black horizontal line represents the highway, with two labeled points on it: A toward the middle and B at the far right. Two gray dashed sight lines drop from the airplane to those points, the line to A being the steeper of the pair and the line to B running much shallower because B lies farther off. Arcs drawn at the airplane mark the two angles opening downward from the dashed horizontal, labeled 25 degrees for the shallow line toward B and 49 degrees for the steep line toward A. Sharing a single vertex for both angles of depression turns the two sight lines and the road into a pair of triangles with a common side. The arrangement supports solving for the airplane's slant distance to A and its elevation above the road once the spacing between the two mileposts is supplied.

interactionPlan.concept: An angle of depression is measured down from the horizontal at the observer, and two such sightings from one airplane to two points on a straight road create two right triangles that share the same altitude leg — which is what lets you solve for the plane's height and slant distances.
elements: Small jetliner icon at upper left, nose pointed left, serving as the common vertex of both sight lines
Teal dashed horizontal reference line extending right from the airplane at flight altitude
Solid black horizontal line across the lower portion representing the straight highway
Point marker and label 'A' on the highway, toward the middle
Point marker and label 'B' on the highway, at the far right
Gray dashed sight line from airplane down to A (steeper)
Gray dashed sight line from airplane down to B (shallower)
Angle arc at the airplane between the teal horizontal and the sight line to B, labeled '25°'
Angle arc at the airplane between the teal horizontal and the sight line to A, labeled '49°'
Vertical dashed altitude segment from the airplane down to the highway (appears in later phases), labeled h
Right-angle square where the altitude segment meets the highway
Horizontal ground distance brackets: airplane's ground point to A, and A to B labeled 'AB'
Slant distance labels along the sight lines (distance to A, distance to B), shown in the unknowns phase
Equation callout box showing tan(49°) = h / x_A and tan(25°) = h / (x_A + AB)
Legend / color key: teal = horizontal reference, gray dashed = lines of sight, black = highway, orange = unknown quantities

interactions.label: Airplane altitude h (miles)
interactions.teaches: Raising the plane steepens BOTH sight lines at once, so both depression angles grow together — the two angles are not independent, they are locked to a single shared height.

interactions.label: Distance from A to B along the highway (miles)
interactions.teaches: Sliding B farther down the road flattens only the far sight line and shrinks only the 25° angle, showing that the gap AB is exactly the quantity that ties the two right triangles together.

interactions.label: Solution stage
interactions.teaches: The standard setup for an angle-of-depression problem: measure angles from the horizontal, drop an altitude to create right triangles, name the unknown horizontal legs, then write one tangent equation per triangle.

demo_steps.title: The horizontal reference
demo_steps.narration: Angles of depression are always measured downward from the horizontal through the observer, not from the ground. The teal dashed line is that horizontal; the sight line to A drops 49° below it and the sight line to B only 25°.

demo_steps.title: Drop the altitude: two right triangles
demo_steps.narration: Dropping a perpendicular from the plane to the highway splits the picture into two right triangles that share the same vertical leg h. The nearer, steeper sighting gives the small triangle; the farther, shallower one gives the large triangle.

demo_steps.title: Name the unknowns
demo_steps.narration: The horizontal leg to A is x, so the horizontal leg to B is x + AB. Only the spacing between the mileposts is known — everything orange is unknown.

demo_steps.title: Raise the plane
demo_steps.narration: Push the altitude up and watch both angles open wider simultaneously. One height controls both triangles, which is precisely why two sightings are enough to pin it down.

demo_steps.title: Push B down the road
demo_steps.narration: Now hold the height fixed and slide B away. Only the far angle changes, collapsing toward the horizontal — the 25° reading is really a statement about how far B is, given the same h.

demo_steps.title: Two tangents, one system
demo_steps.narration: tan(49°) = h/x and tan(25°) = h/(x + AB). Two equations, two unknowns: eliminate x to get h = AB / (cot 25° − cot 49°), then recover the slant distance to A.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Both sight lines leave the same airplane, so the two right triangles share one vertical leg — the shared altitude is the bridge that converts two depression angles and one known ground gap into every missing distance.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape scene. Upper left: a small stylized blue-gray jetliner with nose pointing left; its nose/tail region is the common vertex for all rays. From that vertex a teal dashed horizontal line runs all the way to the right edge. A solid black horizontal line near the bottom spans most of the width as the highway, with a dot and serif italic label 'A' around the middle-right and 'B' near the far right. Two medium-gray dashed rays run from the airplane vertex down to A and to B; the A-ray is noticeably steeper. Two thin black arcs at the vertex open downward from the teal line, the inner/smaller arc labeled '25°' (to B) and the outer arc labeled '49°' (to A), with the 25° label above and left of the 49° label as in the original. In later phases add a thin dashed vertical segment from the plane straight down to the road with a small right-angle square at its foot and the label h, plus horizontal dimension brackets for x (plane's ground point to A) and AB (A to B); render unknown labels in orange and known ones in black. The equation phase shows a light callout box on the right with tan(49°) = h/x and tan(25°) = h/(x + AB). Keep geometry live: angle arcs, ray slopes, and B's position must all recompute from the altitude and AB sliders, with defaults chosen so the displayed angles read ≈49° and ≈25°.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for airplane altitude: the learner raises or lowers the airplane while A and B stay on the highway, the sight lines and depression angles update, and altitude is tied to the tangent ratios in both right triangles.
- Slider for distance between A and B: the learner moves point B along the road, the shallower sight line and 25 degree angle adjust, and the shared-altitude constraint linking the two triangles becomes clear.

authoredContext:
A pilot is flying over a straight highway. He determines the angles of depression to two mileposts, 2.1 km apart, to be 25° and 49°, as shown in the figure. Find the distance of the plane from point A and the elevation of the plane.

Diagram of a plane flying over a highway. It is to the left and above points A and B on the ground in that order. There is a horizontal line going through the plan parallel to the ground. The angle formed by the horizontal line, the plane, and the line from the plane to point B is 25 degrees. The angle formed by the horizontal line, the plane, and point A is 49 degrees.

discrepancies: The 25° angle label sits very tight against the airplane tail and the upper sight line, and both angle arcs are drawn at noticeably smaller radii than in the source, making the two wedges cramped and harder to read than the clearly separated 25°/49° annotations in the original.
Filled black dots are added at A and B; the source shows only the bare tick-free road with italic letters A and B beneath it.

The airplane glyph is a simplified polygon assembly that reads smaller and flatter than the source's larger 3/4-view jet, and the vertex dot for the sight lines is drawn on the plane body (extra mark not in the source).

Proportions differ slightly: in the source B sits essentially at the far right end of the highway with the teal dashed line running past it to the edge; in the generated figure B sits well inside the road with a long empty segment to its right.

Angle labels are rendered as rounded integers from live geometry, so stepping the altitude slider replaces the canonical '25°/49°' values with other numbers (fine pedagogically, but the figure's identifying labels are not pinned in non-default states).
evaluation.notes: Default state is a faithful, correctly-oriented reproduction of the depression-angle figure (teal horizontal, two gray dashed sight lines, 25°/49° arcs, highway with A and B), backed by genuinely useful sliders, a solution-stage toggle and a 6-step walkthrough; main weaknesses are cramped, slightly small angle annotations near the plane and a few added marks (vertex dot, point dots) plus proportion drift in B's placement.

feedback.rationale: No failure modes or action items remain and all dimensions score 4-5 with a faithful, functional interactive figure; only minor cosmetic nits persist.
